claim: P granules are RNA granules in the C. elegans germ plasm.
source: Here, we characterize the transcriptome and assembly of P granules, RNA granules in the C. elegans germ plasm.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about P granules presented in the abstract.

claim: P granules recruit mRNAs by condensation with the disordered protein MEG-3.
source: We find that P granules recruit mRNAs by condensation with the disordered protein MEG-3.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: MEG-3 traps mRNAs into non-dynamic condensates in vitro.
source: MEG-3 traps mRNAs into non-dynamic condensates in vitro and binds to ~500 mRNAs in vivo in a sequence-independent manner that favors embryonic mRNAs with low ribosome coverage.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro condensation experiments and FRAP data shown in the manuscript.

claim: MEG-3 binds to ~500 mRNAs in vivo.
source: MEG-3 traps mRNAs into non-dynamic condensates in vitro and binds to ~500 mRNAs in vivo in a sequence-independent manner that favors embryonic mRNAs with low ribosome coverage.
evidence: This is supported by iCLIP experimental data identifying 657 MEG-3-bound transcripts.

claim: MEG-3 binds mRNAs in a sequence-independent manner.
source: MEG-3 traps mRNAs into non-dynamic condensates in vitro and binds to ~500 mRNAs in vivo in a sequence-independent manner that favors embryonic mRNAs with low ribosome coverage.
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of iCLIP data and in vitro condensation experiments with various RNA sequences.

claim: MEG-3 binding favors embryonic mRNAs with low ribosome coverage.
source: MEG-3 traps mRNAs into non-dynamic condensates in vitro and binds to ~500 mRNAs in vivo in a sequence-independent manner that favors embryonic mRNAs with low ribosome coverage.
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data showing MEG-3-bound transcripts have lower ribosome occupancy.

claim: Translational stress causes additional mRNAs to localize to P granules.
source: Translational stress causes additional mRNAs to localize to P granules and translational activation correlates with P granule exit for two mRNAs coding for germ cell fate regulators.
evidence: This is supported by heat shock and drug treatment experiments showing recruitment of non-P granule transcripts to P granules.

claim: Translational activation correlates with P granule exit for two mRNAs coding for germ cell fate regulators.
source: Translational stress causes additional mRNAs to localize to P granules and translational activation correlates with P granule exit for two mRNAs coding for germ cell fate regulators.
evidence: This is supported by data on nos-2 and Y51F10.2 showing they exit P granules when translated in P4.

claim: Localization to P granules is not required for translational repression.
source: Localization to P granules is not required for translational repression but is required to enrich mRNAs in the germ lineage for robust germline development.
evidence: This is supported by experiments in meg-3 meg-4 mutants showing translational repression is maintained without P granules.

claim: Localization to P granules is required to enrich mRNAs in the germ lineage for robust germline development.
source: Localization to P granules is not required for translational repression but is required to enrich mRNAs in the germ lineage for robust germline development.
evidence: This is supported by genetic experiments showing synthetic sterility in meg-3 meg-4 mutants combined with loss of germ cell fate regulators.

claim: Intrinsically-disordered proteins drive RNA condensation during P granule assembly.
source: Our observations reveal similarities between P granules and stress granules and identify intrinsically-disordered proteins as drivers of RNA condensation during P granule assembly.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation experiments with MEG-3 and RNA.

claim: RNA granules form by phase separation.
source: RNA granules form by phase separation, a de-mixing process that drives condensation of RNA and proteins into liquid or gel-like phases (Kato et al., 2012; Weber and Brangwynne, 2012; Hyman et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2015; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017; Boeynaems et al., 2018; Mittag and Parker, 2018; Alberti et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on phase separation.

claim: Intrinsically-disordered domains in RNA-binding proteins mediate labile, multivalent protein-protein interactions that drive phase separation in vitro.
source: Intrinsically-disordered domains in RNA-binding proteins mediate labile, multivalent protein-protein interactions that drive phase separation in vitro (Kato et al., 2012; Banani et al., 2017; Shin and Brangwynne, 2017; Boeynaems et al., 2018; Mittag and Parker, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RNA drives phase separation by acting as a scaffold for multivalent RNA-binding proteins or by participating in intermolecular RNA:RNA interactions.
source: RNA also drives phase separation by acting as a scaffold for multivalent RNA-binding proteins or by participating in intermolecular RNA:RNA interactions (Van Treeck and Parker, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Total RNA extracted from yeast cells phase separates in vitro in the absence of any proteins.
source: Total RNA extracted from yeast cells phase separates in vitro in the absence of any proteins (Van Treeck et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Phase separation of 'naked RNA' has been proposed to drive the assembly of stress granules.
source: Phase separation of 'naked RNA' has been proposed to drive the assembly of stress granules, RNA granules that form under conditions of translational stress when thousands of mRNA molecules are released from polysomes (Bounedjah et al., 2014; Van Treeck and Parker, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Embryonic P granules are heterogeneous assemblies that contain at least two phases with distinct dynamics.
source: Embryonic P granules are heterogeneous assemblies (Wang et al., 2014) that contain at least two phases with distinct dynamics: a liquid phase assembled by the RGG domain proteins PGL-1 and its paralog PGL-3 (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Updike et al., 2011; Hanazawa et al., 2011; Saha et al., 2016), and a supporting gel-like phase, assembled by the intrinsically-disordered protein MEG-3 and its paralog MEG-4 (Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature including the authors' own work.

claim: A liquid phase is assembled by the RGG domain proteins PGL-1 and its paralog PGL-3.
source: Embryonic P granules are heterogeneous assemblies (Wang et al., 2014) that contain at least two phases with distinct dynamics: a liquid phase assembled by the RGG domain proteins PGL-1 and its paralog PGL-3 (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Updike et al., 2011; Hanazawa et al., 2011; Saha et al., 2016), and a supporting gel-like phase, assembled by the intrinsically-disordered protein MEG-3 and its paralog MEG-4 (Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A gel-like phase is assembled by the intrinsically-disordered protein MEG-3 and its paralog MEG-4.
source: Embryonic P granules are heterogeneous assemblies (Wang et al., 2014) that contain at least two phases with distinct dynamics: a liquid phase assembled by the RGG domain proteins PGL-1 and its paralog PGL-3 (Brangwynne et al., 2009; Updike et al., 2011; Hanazawa et al., 2011; Saha et al., 2016), and a supporting gel-like phase, assembled by the intrinsically-disordered protein MEG-3 and its paralog MEG-4 (Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: MEG-3 forms small, non-dynamic condensates (<500 nanometers) that associate with the surface of larger, dynamic PGL condensates (>500 nanometers).
source: MEG-3 forms small, non-dynamic condensates (<500 nanometers) that associate with the surface of larger, dynamic PGL condensates (>500 nanometers).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: MEG condensates enrich in the posterior cytoplasm of zygotes where they recruit and stabilize PGL condensates inherited from the oocyte.
source: MEG condensates enrich in the posterior cytoplasm of zygotes where they recruit and stabilize PGL condensates inherited from the oocyte (Wang et al., 2014; Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: P granules contain polyadenylated mRNAs.
source: P granules contain polyadenylated mRNAs (Seydoux and Fire, 1994), but so far only four mRNAs have been reported to localize to P granules in embryos (pos-1, mex-1, gld-1 and nos-2; (Subramaniam and Seydoux, 1999; Schisa et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Only four mRNAs have been reported to localize to P granules in embryos (pos-1, mex-1, gld-1 and nos-2).
source: P granules contain polyadenylated mRNAs (Seydoux and Fire, 1994), but so far only four mRNAs have been reported to localize to P granules in embryos (pos-1, mex-1, gld-1 and nos-2; (Subramaniam and Seydoux, 1999; Schisa et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: nos-2 codes for a homolog of the conserved germline determinant Nanos that specifies germ cell fate redundantly with nos-1.
source: nos-2 codes for a homolog of the conserved germline determinant Nanos that specifies germ cell fate redundantly with nos-1, another Nanos homolog expressed later in development (Subramaniam and Seydoux, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: 657 transcripts were identified that were reproducibly recovered above the GFP background threshold in two independent MEG-3::GFP iCLIP experiments.
source: We identified 657 transcripts that were reproducibly recovered above the GFP background threshold in two independent MEG-3::GFP iCLIP experiments ('MEG-3-bound transcripts'; Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by iCLIP experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Only 18 transcripts were identified above background in the two PGL-1::GFP iCLIPs.
source: In contrast, we identified only 18 transcripts above background in the two PGL-1::GFP iCLIPs, despite abundant PGL-1::GFP protein in the immunoprecipitates (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by iCLIP experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 15/18 of the PGL-1-bound transcripts were also in the MEG-3-bound list.
source: 15/18 of the PGL-1-bound transcripts were also in the MEG-3-bound list (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of iCLIP data.

claim: MEG-3 binds a specific subset of mRNAs.
source: We compared the average normalized read count (RPKM) across the two iCLIPs to transcript abundance in P blastomeres (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) or in whole embryos (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and detected no strong correlation, suggesting that MEG-3 binds a specific subset of mRNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from lack of correlation between iCLIP reads and transcript abundance.

claim: Low abundance mRNAs were underrepresented in the iCLIPs.
source: Low abundance mRNAs, however, were underrepresented in the iCLIPs and therefore could have been missed in our analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is observed from the data distribution in the figures.

claim: nos-2, pos-1, mex-1 and gld-1 were among the MEG-3-bound transcripts.
source: Among the MEG-3-bound transcripts were nos-2, pos-1, mex-1 and gld-1, the four transcripts previously reported to localize to P granules (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by iCLIP data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: A strong correlation (R = 0.92) was observed between average raw read count in the MEG-3::GFP iCLIPs and average granule size determined by smFISH.
source: For each transcript, we determined the average granule size in the P2 blastomere and compared that to the average raw read count in the MEG-3::GFP iCLIPs and observed a strong correlation (R = 0.92) (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 18 transcripts among the 492-gene set predicted to localize to P granules were examined and all localized robustly to P granules.
source: In total, we examined 18 transcripts among this 492-gene set and found that, as predicted, all localized robustly to P granules (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in the figures.

claim: Only 21 ± 3% puf-5 molecules localized to P granules in the P2 blastomere.
source: We found that only 21 ± 3% puf-5 and 34 ± 3% Y51F10.2 molecules localized to P granules in the P2 blastomere.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative smFISH analysis.

claim: Only 34 ± 3% Y51F10.2 molecules localized to P granules in the P2 blastomere.
source: We found that only 21 ± 3% puf-5 and 34 ± 3% Y51F10.2 molecules localized to P granules in the P2 blastomere.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative smFISH analysis.

claim: P granules occupy 5.9 ± 2% of the P2 cell volume.
source: Because P granules occupy only a small portion of the P2 cell volume (5.9 ± 2%), this enrichment corresponds to a ~ 6 fold increase in concentration over the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging analysis.

claim: nos-2 mRNA still localized to granules in embryos lacking pgl-1 and pgl-3.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, nos-2 mRNA still localized to granules in embryos lacking pgl-1 and pgl-3, but not in embryos lacking meg-3 and meg-4 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data in mutant embryos shown in Figure 1F.

claim: nos-2 mRNA did not localize to granules in embryos lacking meg-3 and meg-4.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, nos-2 mRNA still localized to granules in embryos lacking pgl-1 and pgl-3, but not in embryos lacking meg-3 and meg-4 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data in mutant embryos shown in Figure 1F.

claim: nos-2 and Y51F10.2 still localized to P granules in embryos lacking the PIWI-class Argonaute PRG-1.
source: We found that nos-2 and Y51F10.2 still localized to P granules in embryos lacking the PIWI-class Argonaute PRG-1 (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data in prg-1 mutant embryos.

claim: mRNA recruitment to embryonic P granules depends on MEG-3 and MEG-4.
source: We conclude that mRNA recruitment to embryonic P granules depends on MEG-3 and MEG-4 and does not require PGL-1 and PGL-3 or the Argonaute PRG-1.
evidence: This is concluded from genetic experiments in various mutant backgrounds.

claim: mRNA recruitment to embryonic P granules does not require PGL-1 and PGL-3.
source: We conclude that mRNA recruitment to embryonic P granules depends on MEG-3 and MEG-4 and does not require PGL-1 and PGL-3 or the Argonaute PRG-1.
evidence: This is concluded from genetic experiments in various mutant backgrounds.

claim: mRNA recruitment to embryonic P granules does not require the Argonaute PRG-1.
source: We conclude that mRNA recruitment to embryonic P granules depends on MEG-3 and MEG-4 and does not require PGL-1 and PGL-3 or the Argonaute PRG-1.
evidence: This is concluded from genetic experiments in various mutant backgrounds.

claim: The majority of reads in the MEG-3::GFP iCLIPs mapped to protein-coding mRNA transcripts.
source: The majority of reads in the MEG-3::GFP iCLIPs mapped to protein-coding mRNA transcripts (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of iCLIP sequencing data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: MEG-3 binds transcripts throughout the coding and UTR regions, with a preference for 3'UTR sequences.
source: Metagene analysis of the MEG-3::GFP toeprints revealed that MEG-3 binds transcripts throughout the coding and UTR regions, with a preference for 3'UTR sequences (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by metagene analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: No evidence for any sequence preference was found in the MEG-3 toeprints.
source: We analyzed the MEG-3 toeprints for possible motifs and found no evidence for any sequence preference (Materials and methods).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of iCLIP data.

claim: MEG-3-bound transcripts tended to be longer on average than other embryonic transcripts.
source: MEG-3-bound transcripts tended to be longer on average than other embryonic transcripts (Figure 2B) and were enriched for transcripts known to be targeted by translational repressors expressed in oocytes, including OMA-1, GLD-1 and LIN-41 and CGH-1 (Boag et al., 2008; Scheckel et al., 2012; Tsukamoto et al., 2017) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: MEG-3-bound transcripts were enriched for transcripts known to be targeted by translational repressors expressed in oocytes, including OMA-1, GLD-1 and LIN-41 and CGH-1.
source: MEG-3-bound transcripts tended to be longer on average than other embryonic transcripts (Figure 2B) and were enriched for transcripts known to be targeted by translational repressors expressed in oocytes, including OMA-1, GLD-1 and LIN-41 and CGH-1 (Boag et al., 2008; Scheckel et al., 2012; Tsukamoto et al., 2017) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis with published datasets shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MEG-3-bound transcripts are on average less protected by ribosomes than other embryonic transcripts.
source: Ribosome profiling experiments confirmed that MEG-3-bound transcripts are on average less protected by ribosomes than other embryonic transcripts (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A for P granule transcripts).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 65% of mRNAs with the lowest ribosome occupancy class (ribosome occupancy <0.1) were among the 'P granule transcripts' set.
source: We identified 19 mRNAs that ranked in the lowest ribosome occupancy class (ribosome occupancy <0.1; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B). 65% of these mRNAs were among the 'P granule transcripts' set defined above, including cbd-1 which strongly localizes to P granules (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A brief incubation at 30°C (15 min heat shock) was sufficient to disassemble polysomes in embryos.
source: We found that a brief incubation at 30°C (15 min heat shock) was sufficient to disassemble polysomes in embryos (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C) (McCormick and Penman, 1969; Shalgi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: All five non-P granule transcripts analyzed accumulated in P granules after heat shock.
source: We analyzed five non-P granule transcripts, chosen for their high ribosome occupancy under non-heat shock conditions, and remarkably found that all five accumulated in P granules after heat shock (Figure 2D–E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data before and after heat shock shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Accumulation in P granules after heat shock was observed in wild-type embryos, but not in embryos depleted of MEG proteins.
source: Accumulation in P granules was observed in wild-type embryos, but not in embryos depleted of MEG proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data in mutant embryos shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: MEG-3::GFP condensates became larger upon heat shock.
source: We noticed that MEG-3::GFP condensates became larger upon heat shock.
evidence: This is observed from imaging data.

claim: Treatment with puromycin increased the size of MEG-3::GFP granules by ~4 fold.
source: We found that treatment with puromycin, which causes ribosomes to dissociate from transcripts, increased the size of MEG-3::GFP granules by ~4 fold, as also observed following heat-shock (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: Treatment with cycloheximide did not change the size of MEG-3::GFP granules.
source: In contrast, treatment with cycloheximide, which stalls ribosomes on transcripts, did not change the size of MEG-3::GFP granules (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 2F and G.

claim: The divergent effect of puromycin and cycloheximide on MEG-3 granules parallels their effect on the assembly of stress granules.
source: These findings parallel the divergent effect of puromycin and cycloheximide on the assembly of stress granules (Kedersha et al., 2000; Aulas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to published literature on stress granules.

claim: nos-2 and Y51F10.2 transitioned to a more diffuse cytoplasmic localization in the germline founder cell P4.
source: Among the 18 P granule transcripts analyzed by in situ hybridization, we noticed two (nos-2 and Y51F10.2) that transitioned to a more diffuse cytoplasmic localization in the last P blastomere, the germline founder cell P4 (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: nos-2 codes for a Nanos homolog that becomes translated in P4.
source: As mentioned above, nos-2 codes for a Nanos homolog that becomes translated in P4 (Subramaniam and Seydoux, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Y51F10.2 is translated specifically in P4.
source: We tagged the Y51F10.2 open reading frame with a small epitope by genome editing, and found that like nos-2, Y51F10.2 is translated specifically in P4 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: nos-2 translation is repressed prior to the P4 stage by the RNA-binding protein MEX-3 and activated in P4 by the RNA-binding protein POS-1.
source: nos-2 translation is regulated by proteins that compete for binding to the nos-2 3' UTR (Jadhav et al., 2008). In particular, translation is repressed prior to the P4 stage by the RNA-binding protein MEX-3 and activated in P4 by the RNA-binding protein POS-1 (Jadhav et al., 2008) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Y51F10.2 translation is repressed prior to the P4 stage by MEX-3 and activated in P4 by POS-1.
source: We found that the same is true for Y51F10.2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data in mex-3 and pos-1 RNAi embryos shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In mex-3(RNAi) embryos, nos-2 and Y51F10.2 mRNAs did not localize to P granules.
source: In mex-3(RNAi) embryos, nos-2 and Y51F10.2 mRNAs did not localize to P granules.
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data in mex-3 RNAi embryos shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: In pos-1(RNAi) embryos, nos-2 and Y51F10.2 mRNAs remained in P granules through P4.
source: In contrast, in pos-1(RNAi) embryos, nos-2 and Y51F10.2 mRNAs remained in P granules through P4 (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data in pos-1 RNAi embryos shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The translational timing of nos-2 and Y51F10.2 was unaffected in meg-3 meg-4 mutants.
source: Surprisingly, we found that the translational timing of nos-2 and Y51F10.2 was unaffected in meg-3 meg-4 mutants. nos-2 and Y51F10.2 were translationally silent prior to the P4 stage and began translation in P4 in meg-3 meg-4 mutants as in wild-type (Figure 3A,B), although protein levels appeared reduced (see below).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data in meg-3 meg-4 mutants shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: MEG-3-bound transcripts as a class maintained low ribosome occupancy in meg-3 meg-4 mutants as in wild-type.
source: We found that MEG-3-bound transcripts as a class maintained low ribosome occupancy in meg-3 meg-4 mutants as in wild-type (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data in meg-3 meg-4 mutants shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Only 25 embryonic mRNAs showed differential ribosomal occupancy in meg-3 meg-4 embryos versus wild-type.
source: Only 25 embryonic mRNAs showed differential ribosomal occupancy in meg-3 meg-4 embryos versus wild-type, and strikingly most showed lower ribosome occupancy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by differential ribosome profiling analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Neither localization to P granules nor binding to MEG-3 is a requirement for translational silencing.
source: These results confirm that neither localization to P granules nor binding to MEG-3 is a requirement for translational silencing.
evidence: This is concluded from ribosome profiling data in meg-3 meg-4 mutants.

claim: Translation silencing appears to be a requirement for localization to P granules.
source: Translation silencing, however, appears to be a requirement for localization to P granules, with translational activation correlating with P granule exit.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between translational status and P granule localization.

claim: nos-2 and Y51F10.2 transcript and protein levels were lower in the germline founder cell P4 in meg-3 meg-4 mutants compared to wild-type.
source: We noticed that nos-2 and Y51F10.2 transcript and protein levels were lower in the germline founder cell P4 in meg-3 meg-4 mutants compared to wild-type (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is observed from smFISH and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: In wild-type embryos, P granule-associated mRNAs segregate preferentially to germline blastomeres with the P granules during each asymmetric division.
source: In wild-type embryos, P granule-associated mRNAs segregate preferentially to germline blastomeres with the P granules during each asymmetric division (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is observed from smFISH data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: In meg-3 meg-4 mutants, P granule-associated mRNAs segregate symmetrically at each division.
source: In contrast, in meg-3 meg-4 mutants, P granule-associated mRNAs segregate symmetrically at each division, resulting in lower levels in germline blastomeres compared to wild-type (Figure 3A–B).
evidence: This is observed from smFISH data in meg-3 meg-4 mutants shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: P granule transcripts were present on average at lower levels overall in meg-3 meg-4 embryos compared to wild-type.
source: As expected for equal segregation to somatic blastomeres followed by degradation, we found that P granule transcripts were present on average at lower levels overall in meg-3 meg-4 embryos compared to wild-type as determined by RNAseq (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 30% of meg-3 meg-4 mutants develop into sterile adults.
source: 30% of meg-3 meg-4 mutants develop into sterile adults (Figure 3D) (Wang et al., 2014), raising the possibility that failure to enrich maternal mRNAs in the germline founder cell P4 compromises germline development.
evidence: This is supported by sterility data shown in Figure 3D and citation to previous literature.

claim: Embryos derived from mothers carrying deletions in nos-2 or Y51F10.2 were close to 100% fertile.
source: Embryos derived from mothers carrying deletions in nos-2 or Y51F10.2 were close to 100% fertile (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by sterility data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Y51F10.2; nos-2 double mutant mothers laid 46 ± 15% sterile progeny that lacked a germline.
source: In contrast, Y51F10.2; nos-2 double mutant mothers laid 46 ± 15% sterile progeny that lacked a germline (maternal-effect sterility), suggesting that Y51F10.2 functions redundantly with nos-2 in germ cell fate specification (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by sterility data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Y51F10.2 functions redundantly with nos-2 in germ cell fate specification.
source: In contrast, Y51F10.2; nos-2 double mutant mothers laid 46 ± 15% sterile progeny that lacked a germline (maternal-effect sterility), suggesting that Y51F10.2 functions redundantly with nos-2 in germ cell fate specification (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic interaction data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The majority of nos-2; meg-3 meg-4 and Y51F10.2; meg-3 meg-4 triple mutants grew into sterile animals lacking a germline.
source: Remarkably, the majority of nos-2; meg-3 meg-4 and Y51F10.2; meg-3 meg-4 triple mutants grew into sterile animals lacking a germline (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by sterility data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The primary function of the MEG-3 phase is to preferentially segregate maternal mRNAs to the germline founder cell P4 to ensure robust germ cell specification.
source: We conclude that the primary function of the MEG-3 phase is to preferentially segregate maternal mRNAs to the germline founder cell P4 to ensure robust germ cell specification.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic and molecular data presented.

claim: The MEG-3 phase is NOT essential for translational silencing.
source: Importantly, the MEG-3 phase is NOT essential for translational silencing or for preferential stabilization of maternal mRNAs in germline blastomeres compared to somatic blastomeres.
evidence: This is concluded from ribosome profiling and RNA stability data in meg-3 meg-4 mutants.

claim: The MEG-3 phase is NOT essential for preferential stabilization of maternal mRNAs in germline blastomeres compared to somatic blastomeres.
source: Importantly, the MEG-3 phase is NOT essential for translational silencing or for preferential stabilization of maternal mRNAs in germline blastomeres compared to somatic blastomeres.
evidence: This is concluded from RNA stability data in meg-3 meg-4 mutants.

claim: Recombinant MEG-3 readily condenses with total RNA extracted from C. elegans embryos.
source: We showed previously that recombinant MEG-3 readily condenses with total RNA extracted from C. elegans embryos (Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: All nine transcripts tested stimulated the formation of MEG-3 condensates and became enriched in the condensates with similar efficiencies.
source: We found that all nine transcripts stimulated the formation of MEG-3 condensates and became enriched in the condensates with similar efficiencies (Figure 4B–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation assay data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: No RNA condensates were observed in the absence of MEG-3 even at high RNA concentrations (80 ng/µL).
source: We observed no RNA condensates in the absence of MEG-3 even at high RNA concentrations (80 ng/µL), confirming that our conditions do not induce RNA-only aggregation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: MEG-3 has a predicted pI of 9.3.
source: MEG-3 has a predicted pI of 9.3 (ExPASy) and thus could potentially interact with the sugar-phosphate backbone of RNA through electrostatic interactions.
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using ExPASy.

claim: In the absence of RNA, MEG-3 formed aggregates under all salt concentrations tested.
source: In the absence of RNA, MEG-3 formed aggregates under all salt concentrations tested (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In high salt (500 mM) conditions, MEG-3 continued to form aggregates even in the presence of nos-2 RNA and these aggregates did not recruit nos-2 RNA.
source: In high salt (500 mM) conditions, MEG-3 continued to form aggregates even in the presence of nos-2 RNA and these aggregates did not recruit nos-2 RNA (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: At the lowest concentrations of NaCl, high concentrations of RNA caused MEG-3 to solubilize with no visible aggregates or condensates.
source: Remarkably, at the lowest concentrations of NaCl, high concentrations of RNA caused MEG-3 to solubilize with no visible aggregates or condensates (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2D,F,G).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Short RNAs (30 and 100 nt) were not as efficient as longer RNAs at stimulating MEG-3 condensation.
source: We found that short RNAs (30 and 100 nt) were not as efficient as longer RNAs at stimulating MEG-3 condensation (Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro condensation assay data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: MEG-3 protein becomes immobilized in MEG-3/RNA condensates, with no MEG-3 exchange detected within one minute of condensation.
source: We previously showed that MEG-3 protein becomes immobilized in MEG-3/RNA condensates, with no MEG-3 exchange detected within one minute of condensation (Putnam et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Short RNAs (30 and 100 nt) were mobile in MEG-3 condensates.
source: We found that short RNAs (30 and 100 nt) were mobile in MEG-3 condensates.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Longer RNAs (200 nt and higher), including four full-length transcripts, exhibited no detectable exchange in MEG-3 condensates.
source: In contrast, longer RNAs (200 nt and higher), including four full-length transcripts, exhibited no detectable exchange (Figure 5C,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experiments shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: MEG-3 interacts most efficiently with mRNA-sized RNAs, which become trapped in the MEG-3 condensates.
source: We conclude that MEG-3 interacts most efficiently with mRNA-sized RNAs, which become trapped in the MEG-3 condensates.
evidence: This is concluded from the RNA length-dependent condensation and FRAP data.

claim: MEG-3 granules remained positive for SYTO 14 ex vivo for over 1.5 min.
source: We found that MEG-3 granules remained positive for SYTO 14 ex vivo for over 1.5 min (the maximum time tested; Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo extrusion experiments shown in Figure 5E,F.

claim: The majority of RNAs in embryonic P granules do not reside in the PGL phase.
source: These observations indicate that mRNAs associate stably with the MEG phase ex vivo as observed in vitro, and confirm that the majority of RNAs in embryonic P granules do not reside in the PGL phase.
evidence: This is concluded from the ex vivo stability experiments and comparison to PGL phase behavior.

claim: The PGL phase of P granules is neither necessary nor sufficient for RNA recruitment to embryonic P granules.
source: In this study, we demonstrate that the PGL phase of P granules is neither necessary not sufficient for RNA recruitment to embryonic P granules, which occurs through an independent gel-like phase organized by MEG-3 (and its paralog MEG-4).
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic and molecular data presented.

claim: mRNAs are recruited to P granules by direct binding to MEG proteins.
source: Several lines of evidence indicate that mRNAs are recruited to P granules by direct binding to MEG proteins.
evidence: This is concluded from multiple lines of evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: iCLIP experiments demonstrate a strong correlation between MEG-3-binding and P granule localization.
source: First, iCLIP experiments demonstrate a strong correlation between MEG-3-binding and P granule localization (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Localization to granules requires meg-3 and meg-4 and does not require pgl-1 and pgl-3.
source: Second, localization to granules requires meg-3 and meg-4 and does not require pgl-1 and pgl-3 (Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by genetic experiments shown in Figure 1F.

claim: mRNAs in P granules are in a phase that is resistant to dilution and high temperature like the MEG phase and unlike the PGL phase.
source: Third, mRNAs in P granules are in a phase that is resistant to dilution and high temperature like the MEG phase and unlike the PGL phase.
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo extrusion experiments.

claim: MEG-3 binds RNA robustly in vitro and in vivo.
source: Finally, despite lacking a canonical RNA binding domain, MEG-3 binds RNA robustly in vitro (Smith et al., 2016) and in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and properties of MEG-3/RNA condensates assembled in vitro match properties of the MEG phase in vivo (Figure 4 and Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by iCLIP data and in vitro binding assays.

claim: Properties of MEG-3/RNA condensates assembled in vitro match properties of the MEG phase in vivo.
source: Finally, despite lacking a canonical RNA binding domain, MEG-3 binds RNA robustly in vitro (Smith et al., 2016) and in vivo (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and properties of MEG-3/RNA condensates assembled in vitro match properties of the MEG phase in vivo (Figure 4 and Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of in vitro and in vivo data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The MEG phase is gel-like.
source: We previously showed that the MEG phase is gel-like (Putnam et al., 2019) and we demonstrate here that mRNAs become kinetically trapped in the MEG phase.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: mRNAs become kinetically trapped in the MEG phase.
source: We previously showed that the MEG phase is gel-like (Putnam et al., 2019) and we demonstrate here that mRNAs become kinetically trapped in the MEG phase.
evidence: This is supported by FRAP experiments showing no RNA exchange.

claim: Low RNA dynamics have been reported in the germ granules of other organisms.
source: Low RNA dynamics have also been reported in the germ granules of other organisms (Jamieson-Lucy and Mullins, 2019; Trcek and Lehmann, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Specification of the germline using germ granules and other asymmetrically-segregated maternal factors (germ plasm) is a derived trait that arose independently several times during metazoan evolution.
source: Specification of the germline using germ granules and other asymmetrically-segregated maternal factors (germ plasm) is a derived trait that arose independently several times during metazoan evolution (Kulkarni and Extavour, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Proteins that scaffold germ granule assembly in different organisms (Drosophila Oskar, vertebrate Xvelo/Bucky Ball, and C. elegans MEGs) are non-homologous, but all contain predicted intrinsically-disordered domains and form non-dynamic condensates in vitro.
source: Proteins that scaffold germ granule assembly in different organisms DrosophilaOskar, vertebrate Xvelo/Bucky Ball, and C. elegans MEGs) are non-homologous, but all contain predicted intrinsically-disordered domains and form non-dynamic condensates in vitro.
evidence: This is based on comparison of protein properties across species.

claim: Oskar and Bucky Ball bind Nanos RNA in vitro.
source: Oskar and Bucky Ball bind Nanos RNA in vitro (Yang et al., 2015; Krishnakumar et al., 2018), as we show here for MEG-3.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Condensation of disordered protein domains with RNA may be a common driver of germ granule assembly in a wide range of animals.
source: Condensation of disordered protein domains with RNA, therefore, may be a common driver of germ granule assembly in a wide range of animals.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison across species.

claim: Trapping RNAs in a solid, gel-like phase could be beneficial for long term storage of RNAs during oogenesis and for maintaining a pool of maternal mRNAs in germline precursors before the onset of zygotic transcription.
source: Trapping RNAs in a solid, gel-like phase could be beneficial for long term storage of RNAs during oogenesis and for maintaining a pool of maternal mRNAs in germline precursors before the onset of zygotic transcription (P4 stage; Seydoux and Dunn, 1997).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential function.

claim: Recruitment of nos-2 RNA to P granules requires MEX-3.
source: We report here that recruitment of nos-2 RNA to P granules requires MEX-3, a translational repressor that recognizes specific sequences in the nos-2 3' UTR (Jadhav et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by data in mex-3 RNAi embryos and citation to previous literature.

claim: In vertebrate embryos, mRNA recruitment to the Balbiani body depends on 3' UTR sequences recognized by sequence-specific mRNA-binding proteins.
source: Similarly, in vertebrate embryos, mRNA recruitment to the Balbiani body depends on 3' UTR sequences recognized by sequence-specific mRNA-binding proteins (Jamieson-Lucy and Mullins, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila, recruitment to polar granules depends on 3'UTR sequences implicated in translational repression, as well as potential RNA:piRNA and RNA:RNA homotopic interactions.
source: In Drosophila, recruitment to polar granules also depends on 3'UTR sequences implicated in translational repression, as well as potential RNA:piRNA and RNA:RNA homotopic interactions (Trcek and Lehmann, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Stress granules are RNA granules that form in the cytoplasm of stressed cells to store mRNAs that have exited the translational pool.
source: Stress granules are RNA granules that form in the cytoplasm of stressed cells to store mRNAs that have exited the translational pool (Buchan and Parker, 2009; Ivanov et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The stress granule transcriptome favors long mRNAs that are ribosome-depleted.
source: As we report here for P granules, the stress granule transcriptome favors long mRNAs that are ribosome-depleted (Kedersha et al., 2000; Khong et al., 2017; Aulas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Stress granule assembly is enhanced by treatments that release mRNAs from polysomes (heat-shock and puromycin).
source: Stress granule assembly is enhanced by treatments that release mRNAs from polysomes (heat-shock and puromycin), as we show here for P granules.
evidence: This is supported by comparison to stress granule literature and data presented.

claim: Recruitment of mRNAs to stress granules is an inefficient process, with only a minority of molecules for most mRNA species localizing in the granules.
source: Recruitment of mRNAs to stress granules is an inefficient process, with only a minority of molecules for most mRNA species localizing in the granules (Khong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Translational repression is required for localization to stress granules, but stress granules are not required for translational repression or for mRNA stability.
source: Translational repression is required for localization to P granules, but P granules are not required for translational repression or for mRNA stability, as is also true for stress granules (Kedersha et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature on stress granules.

claim: P granules contain proteins also found in stress granules (poly-A binding protein, TIA-1 and the DDX3/LAF-1 RNA helicase).
source: Finally, P granules contain proteins also found in stress granules (poly-A binding protein, TIA-1 and the DDX3/LAF-1 RNA helicase) and P granules interact with P bodies, as do stress granules (Gallo et al., 2008; Shih et al., 2012; Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: P granules interact with P bodies, as do stress granules.
source: Finally, P granules contain proteins also found in stress granules (poly-A binding protein, TIA-1 and the DDX3/LAF-1 RNA helicase) and P granules interact with P bodies, as do stress granules (Gallo et al., 2008; Shih et al., 2012; Elbaum-Garfinkle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Embryonic P granules function downstream of the translational regulation machinery to temporarily hold mRNAs not engaged with ribosomes until their degradation or translation in the germline blastomere P4.
source: Our findings suggest that, like stress granules, embryonic P granules function downstream of the translational regulation machinery to temporarily hold mRNAs not engaged with ribosomes until their degradation or translation in the germline blastomere P4.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data and comparison to stress granules.

claim: P bodies favor translationally repressed mRNAs and recruit additional mRNAs under translational stress.
source: Interestingly, P bodies also have been reported to favor translationally repressed mRNAs and to recruit additional mRNAs under translational stress (Hubstenberger et al., 2017; Matheny et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Low translation may be a common requirement for entry into cytoplasmic granules.
source: Low translation, therefore, may be a common requirement for entry into cytoplasmic granules.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison across different types of RNA granules.

claim: Not all translationally-repressed mRNAs are recruited equally strongly to P granules.
source: Our analyses indicate, however, that not all translationally-repressed mRNAs are recruited equally strongly to P granules.
evidence: This is observed from the data showing variation in P granule localization among low-translation mRNAs.

claim: P granules assemble preferentially in cytoplasm destined for germline blastomeres.
source: A unique characteristic of P granules is their polarized assembly (Strome and Wood, 1982). P granules assemble preferentially in cytoplasm destined for germline blastomeres (Smith et al., 2016) and consequently mRNAs in P granules are preferentially segregated to germline blastomeres during the first embryonic cleavages.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: mRNAs in P granules are preferentially segregated to germline blastomeres during the first embryonic cleavages.
source: A unique characteristic of P granules is their polarized assembly (Strome and Wood, 1982). P granules assemble preferentially in cytoplasm destined for germline blastomeres (Smith et al., 2016) and consequently mRNAs in P granules are preferentially segregated to germline blastomeres during the first embryonic cleavages.
evidence: This is supported by data showing asymmetric segregation of P granule mRNAs.

claim: Over 4 cell divisions, P granule localization boosts mRNA levels in the germline founder cell P4 over what would have been achieved by equal segregation.
source: Because mRNA localization to P granules is inefficient, this enrichment is relatively weak but, over 4 cell divisions, boosts mRNAs levels in the germline founder cell P4 over what would have been achieved by equal segregation.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative data on mRNA segregation.

claim: meg-3 meg-4 mutants segregate P granule mRNAs equally to germline and somatic blastomeres, leading to reduced levels in P4 compared to wild-type.
source: meg-3 meg-4 mutants, which lack P granules, segregate P granule mRNAs equally to germline and somatic blastomeres, leading to reduced levels in P4 compared to wild-type.
evidence: This is supported by smFISH data in meg-3 meg-4 mutants.

claim: meg-3 meg-4 mutants are 30% sterile and exquisitely sensitive to loss of germ cell fate regulators.
source: meg-3 meg-4 mutants are 30% sterile and exquisitely sensitive to loss of germ cell fate regulators.
evidence: This is supported by sterility data and genetic interaction experiments.

claim: Embryonic P granules, while non-essential, are required for robust germ cell fate specification.
source: These observations are consistent with previous studies, which showed that embryonic P granules, while non-essential, are required for robust germ cell fate specification (Gallo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Embryonic P granules are required to maintain small RNA homeostasis across generations, likely via the PGL phase which contains Argonaute proteins and other epigenetic factors.
source: Embryonic P granules are also required to maintain small RNA homeostasis across generations, likely via the PGL phase which contains Argonaute proteins and other epigenetic factors (Ouyang et al., 2019; Dodson and Kennedy, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Embryonic P granules are two-phase, dual-cargo condensates whose main function is to maximize transmission of maternal mRNAs (MEG phase) and epigenetic factors (PGL phase) to the germline founder cell P4.
source: We propose that embryonic P granules are two-phase, dual-cargo condensates whose main function is to maximize transmission of maternal mRNAs (MEG phase) and epigenetic factors (PGL phase) to the germline founder cell P4.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data presented.

claim: P granules are not essential for translational repression or preferential RNA stability in germline blastomeres.
source: Importantly, our findings demonstrate that P granules are not essential for translational repression or preferential RNA stability in germline blastomeres.
evidence: This is concluded from experiments in meg-3 meg-4 mutants.

claim: Y51F10.2 codes for the C. elegans orthologue of human TRIM32, a member of the broadly conserved TRIM-NHL protein family implicated in protein ubiquitination and mRNA regulation.
source: Y51F10.2 codes for the C. elegans orthologue of human TRIM32, a member of the broadly conserved TRIM-NHL protein family implicated in protein ubiquitination and mRNA regulation (Tocchini and Ciosk, 2015).
evidence: This is based on sequence homology and citation to previous literature.

claim: Y51F10.2 functions in germ cell fate specification redundantly with nos-2.
source: Our genetic findings indicate that 1) Y51F10.2 functions in germ cell fate specification redundantly with nos-2 and 2) additional germ cell fate regulators likely exist among the other P granule mRNAs.
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data showing synthetic sterility.

claim: Additional germ cell fate regulators likely exist among the other P granule mRNAs.
source: Our genetic findings indicate that 1) Y51F10.2 functions in germ cell fate specification redundantly with nos-2 and 2) additional germ cell fate regulators likely exist among the other P granule mRNAs.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher penetrance of sterility in certain mutant combinations.

claim: Not all P granule-enriched transcripts function in germ cell specification.
source: It appears unlikely, however, that all P granule-enriched transcripts function in germ cell specification.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that many P granule mRNAs turn over before P4 and some have known functions in other processes.

claim: The MEG phase may serve as a relatively non-specific repository for untranslated or low-translation mRNAs, many of which do not function in germ cell fate specification.
source: The MEG phase, therefore, may serve as a relatively non-specific repository for untranslated or low-translation mRNAs, many of which do not function in germ cell fate specification.
evidence: This is inferred from the data on P granule mRNA composition and function.

claim: The first step for mRNA selection in the Drosophila polar granules has been proposed to rely on a relatively non-specific mechanism involving mRNA:piRNA interactions.
source: It is interesting to note that the first step for mRNA selection in the Drosophila polar granules also has been proposed to rely on a relatively non-specific mechanism, in that case involving mRNA:piRNA interactions (Vourekas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Recruitment of mRNAs to stress granules is mostly non-specific with over 80% of mRNA species recruited.
source: Similarly, recruitment of mRNAs to stress granules is mostly non-specific with over 80% of mRNA species recruited (Khong et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Sequence non-specific RNA condensation may be a common strategy to spatially segregate mRNAs in cells and embryos.
source: Sequence non-specific RNA condensation may therefore be a common strategy to spatially segregate mRNAs in cells and embryos.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison across different RNA granule systems.
